name: Topical estrogen (estriol) cream

lead: Estriol cream is used for thicker, firmer, smoother skin, mostly by older and postmenopausal users. Estriol is a mild natural estrogen, one of the three major endogenous estrogens, available mainly for menopausal hormone therapy.

It activates estrogen receptors more weakly than estradiol, acting as a partial agonist, and skin thickness and collagen are the targets. Wikipedia reports research showing estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen. Trials of facial appearance in other groups were not found.

paras: It is applied as a cream to the skin. Estriol products are sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories and some skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies. Using it on the face is off-label.

It is generally well tolerated; reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia. It is generally prescription-only, and as a hormone product it carries estrogen-class effects.

chain: Estriol acts on skin estrogen receptors
angle.text: Estriol cream is used for thicker, firmer, smoother skin, mostly among older users, as an off-label use of a menopausal hormone ingredient. It acts on skin estrogen receptors, and skin thickness and collagen rise. Research reports it can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen.

lead: Estriol (E3) is a weak natural estrogen, one of the three major endogenous estrogens alongside estradiol and estrone, and is available as a medication mainly for menopausal hormone therapy. It is sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories, and some skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies [1][2].

In appearance circles, estriol cream is discussed as a way to counter the decline in skin thickness and collagen after menopause. Wikipedia reports that research has found estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen [2]. The sources reviewed did not include trial details, and no appearance-specific clinical studies were summarised here.
infobox: Generally prescription-only; some creams OTC or compounded [2]

paras: Estriol activates both estrogen receptors, ER-alpha and ER-beta, but is much less potent than estradiol and acts as a partial agonist, so it can weakly mimic estradiol or partly block it when both are present. It binds poorly to sex hormone-binding globulin and is cleared by glucuronidation and sulfation, mainly through urine [1].

Estriol is used for menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes, vaginal atrophy and painful intercourse, and has been linked to fewer urinary tract infections. Vaginal use is well established, with much higher vaginal than oral bioavailability. Its effects on bone density are described as inconsistent [2]. Skin creams exist as over-the-counter and compounded products, and research is reported to show estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen [2].

Estriol is generally well tolerated. Reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation, burning, itching or discharge with vaginal use. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia, though typical vaginal doses appear to carry little of this risk [2].

Estriol was discovered in 1930, isolated and purified from the urine of pregnant women by Marrian and colleagues, and was introduced for medical use soon after [1][2]. It is generally prescription-only, with Ovestin as the main brand [2].

No studies found in the sources reviewed that specifically test estriol cream for facial appearance in non-menopausal users. Wikipedia states that research shows estriol reverses the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen, without detailing individual trials [2].
